The Yellow-vented bulbul (Pycnonotus goiavier) is a common passerine of Southeast Asian lowlands whose life history traits reflect a strategy adapted to warm, stable thermal environments. Eggs incubated at 40 °C [T = 40 °C] hatch after approximately 12.5 days [ab = approximately 12.5 days], a developmental period consistent with the short incubation durations typical of tropical passerines. Newly hatched nestlings emerge at an initial wet weight of 2.78 grams [Ww0 = 2.78 grams], a modest neonatal mass that underscores the species’ altricial mode of development. This relatively small birth mass places considerable demands on parental provisioning during the nestling phase, as chicks must more than double their body mass within their first week of life to sustain growth trajectories leading to adult dimensions. Field observations of breeding pairs confirm that both parents share brooding and feeding duties intensively during this period, a behavioral pattern that buffers the altricial young against the rapid heat loss and metabolic challenges of the nest environment.

Adult females of Pycnonotus goiavier attain an ultimate wet weight of 28.5 grams [Wwi = 28.5 grams], representing a tenfold increase from the neonatal mass recorded at hatching. This asymptotic body mass is typical of medium-sized pycnonotids and reflects the species’ frugivorous dietary specialization, which provides a lipid-rich nutritional base for sustained somatic growth. Under the elevated body temperatures characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the basal metabolic rate reaches a maximum of 44 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 44 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic value is relatively modest for a passerine of this body size, likely reflecting the energetic efficiencies associated with a fruit-based diet and the thermoregulatory advantages of inhabiting consistently warm climates where daily maintenance costs are relatively low.

The developmental schedule of the yellow-vented bulbul is tightly synchronized with the thermal conditions of its habitat. Under an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging typically occurs at 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching], though published accounts indicate a range of 10 to 14 days depending on local food availability and brood size. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of many tropical passerines and may represent an adaptive response to high nest predation pressure in Southeast Asian ecosystems. Following nest departure, young birds remain dependent on parental food deliveries for several additional weeks before achieving full nutritional independence. Post-fledging survival rates appear to be strongly influenced by the timing of nest emergence relative to peaks in fruit abundance, which vary seasonally across the species’ geographic range.

Reproductive maturation follows a distinct temporal progression under the warm conditions typical of this lowland species (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]). Puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal development and complete plumage maturation, is attained at 36 days after hatching [tp = 36 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. However, the initiation of actual breeding activity occurs considerably later; first brood attempts are not recorded until approximately 401.5 days after hatching [tR = approximately 401.5 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the time required for young birds to secure territories and establish pair bonds in a competitive adult population at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Females lay 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch], a modest clutch size consistent with the low annual reproductive output typical of tropical passerines, and typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year]. This reduced fecundity is compensated by relatively high adult survival and extended breeding tenure, allowing individuals multiple opportunities to reproduce over their lifespan.

Longevity records for Pycnonotus goiavier in natural populations indicate that individuals can survive for up to 11.5 years [am = up to 11.5 years] under the warm thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterize their lowland habitats. This extended lifespan is notable among passerines of comparable body size and likely reflects the species’ generalized foraging ecology, which provides dietary flexibility during periods of resource scarcity. The combination of delayed first reproduction, small clutch sizes, and high adult survival places the yellow-vented bulbul firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum for tropical songbirds, where annual survival rates often exceed 70 percent for territorial adults. Such a strategy is thought to evolve in environments where juvenile mortality is high but adult survival is consistently favorable, allowing even modest annual reproductive output to sustain stable population dynamics over the long term, a pattern that has been documented in several other Southeast Asian pycnonotids.
